author: David Hytner
description:
Armed with an impressive academic record and experience as a rugby fly-half, the teenager is anything but typical

Josh King is talking with pride about how his mother, Michelle, a university lecturer, has almost finished her PhD in sickle cell disease. The Fulham attacking midfielder, who is in the England squad for the Nations League matches against Croatia and Spain this week, mentions that his father, Steve, is a lawyer and says he might have liked to follow in his footsteps if it had not worked out for him on the pitch.

King’s background is not that of a typical footballer. Privately educated at Hampton School in south-west London, he aced his GCSEs, achieving A or A* in his 10 subjects. He went on to study part-time for A-levels in French, maths and psychology, getting grades of A, C and D – pretty impressive, especially when you co
title: Cerebral Josh King plots unusual route into Tuchel’s England plans

author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Gaby Hinsliff ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
Russell Brand, once an award-winning comedian and Hollywood actor, has been sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. The judge paid tribute to the ‘determination and bravery’ of the women who came forward in the case, and described Brand as a sexual predator of ‘staggering arrogance’. Police are investigating two further additional rape allegations and have urged all rape and sexual assault victims to report what happened, ‘no matter how long ago it occured’. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff

Continue reading...
title: Will Russell Brand’s 10-year jail term be a tipping point? - The Latest

author: Gerard Meagher
description:
• Wing Feyi-Waboso sustained ankle injury on Sunday

  • Tom Curry out for rest of November with hip injury

England have been rocked by multiple injury blows after Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry were ruled out of the rest of their autumn campaign. George Furbank, Ollie Chessum and Seb Atkinson are also expected to miss the clash with Japan on Saturday, with the two-try hero Henry Pollock in line for a rare start in a much-changed XV.

Feyi-Waboso sustained an ankle injury in the first half of the 45-22 victory against Australia on Sunday and will miss games against Japan, New Zealand and England’s match on finals weekend. Tom Curry, who sustained a hip injury in training last week, is also out for the rest of November.
title: Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry out of Nations Championship in fresh blow to England

author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey , produced by Luke John Smith and Madelynne Flack, music by Axel Kacoutié ; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
description:
This week the British prime minister will join world leaders in Turkey for the Cop31 summit.

But he may raise some eyebrows as it looks like domestically he is prioritising the cost of living over tackling the climate crisis. The government is set to reduce electric vehicle targets from 80% to 60%, which will please car manufacturers. Meanwhile tensions are still high over the Rosebank oilfield and if it will get the go-ahead.

Should Burnham prioritise the climate over the cost of living?

Continue reading...
title: Cop31: will Andy Burnham choose climate or cost of living? | Politics Weekly

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article about the decline of town centres

Sammy Gecsoyler’s report from Rotherham (‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?, 4 November) tells the story in its dates. One out-of-town retail park in Britain in 1981; 385 by 1996. Parkgate opened in 1987 and MPs warned that it would disembowel towns and villages. It did. Rotherham town centre is now 24% vacant, while retail park vacancy nationally sits at 4.8%. That is not a mystery. It is 40 years of planning policy.

We have since gone one step further by making home delivery cheaper than retail parks. Up to 3bn parcels a year now land on British doorsteps and not one of them passes through a town centre.

Continue reading...
title: How to get the buzz back on Britain’s high streets | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Guardian readers reflect on rail development plans for Digbeth, and on 200 years of musical history – from Duran Duran to the club scene

Regarding your article on the threat to nightlife in Digbeth from proposals by the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance (‘It brings soul into this sterile world’: the Birmingham clubbers fighting to save their patch – and Britain’s nightlife, 3 November), as someone who spends a lot of time in this district of Birmingham, I think it’s also worth recognising that it is getting major investment, turning it into an area you want to visit and even live in.

There are new TV and film studios, street refurbishments, residential flats, a new tram route and better bus services. Access to the area is increasing. The new tram route – wholesale street redesigns, but mothballed until connecting tracks can be laid across HS2’s Curz
title: Is the party ending in Birmingham’s nightlife district? | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Ground-source and air-source heat pumps are extremely efficient machines, writes, David Reynolds

I read Mary Massey’s letter (2 November) with some surprise. She said that her heat pump needs an annual service and that this year it cost about £350. My ground-source heat pump has been heating my house for 18 years and it does not need or get an annual service.

A heat pump is essentially a big refrigerator working in reverse, and how often do you have your fridge serviced? That is another benefit of heat pumps. It has no burner and so it is not continually deteriorating; nor is there a fire-safety issue.

Continue reading...
title: Like fridges, heat pumps don’t need an annual service | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Danielle Metz wonders whether the president will extend the forgiveness he has shown the 6 January insurrectionists to other prisoners, in response to an article by James Rosen

I was granted clemency by President Barack Obama after serving 23 years behind bars (The US founders made a grave error in granting presidents pardon power, 1 November). When I think of clemency, I think about what it was designed to do. How it’s a way to show mercy when those who issued the verdict showed none. Incarcerated people sit in prison for years waiting for someone to show up and correct an obvious wrong. The president and the governor have the power to right that wrong. I can’t imagine it being taken away.

I think back to 6 January 2021, when the Capitol was stormed, and I witnessed the violence and chaos that erupted that day. I remember how frightening it was to watch. Th
title: Obama granted me clemency after 23 years in prison. What will it take for Trump to do similar? | Letter

author: Chris Ward
description:
The world has moved on since 2020 – in uncertain times, closer ties to Europe are the best way to peace and security

  • Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven

If offering the public some “breathing space” in the cost of living crisis was the mantra of last month’s budget, the political space it created to revisit our relationship with the European Union may prove more defining.

I’ve spent what feels like much of the past decade immersed in the Brexit debate – first as an adviser, then helping to craft the red lines that shaped Labour’s 2024 manifesto, and latterly as a Cabinet Office minister working on the EU-reset. In truth, the discussions we have had as a country and within my party on this issue have not really moved on since the moment we left on 31 January 2020.

Chris Ward is Labour MP for Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven
title: I wrote Labour’s Brexit red lines. This is why it’s time to scrap them | Chris Ward

description:
As the UK endured record-breaking temperatures this summer, nothing grew in popularity on Deliveroo like sacks of sweet relief from the supermarket Iceland

Age: The first patents for commercial mechanical production date to the 1850s.

author: Simon Burnton
description:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Precisely 13,266 games have been played since the inception of the Premier League, and 19 of those matches have finished 4-4 (0.1%), a rarity in a division dominated by the mighty 1-0 (17.6%). It was about time we got one, though. The months of August and September, when teams are still fighting to define their top-flight seasons and fitness and motivation tend to be at their peak, have never seen a single 4-4 draw. As motivation decreases the chances of stupid scorelines increase, and that’s where the 4-4 creeps in. There’s a certain on-the-beachness inherent in the score, and it is no coincidence that it has occurred more in the second half of April, as thoughts drift to the close season and the ineffable pointlessness of a lot of late-campaign football becomes unavoidable, than in the entirety of any other month.
title: Football Daily | Manchester United, Aston Villa and the unseriousness of a 4-4 draw

description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics
title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed

author: Ariana Baio
description:
Miller, known as the architect of Trump’s controversial immigration crackdown, is replacing Susie Wiles in new role

  • US politics live – latest updates

Stephen Miller, the architect of Donald Trump’s mass deportation policy and hardline crackdown on immigration, took up his new role as White House chief of staff on Monday.

Miller, 41, began his new role serving as Trump’s right-hand man after Republicans suffered massive losses nationwide in the midterm elections. He was previously serving as a deputy chief of staff.

Continue reading...
title: Hardline Trump aide Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff

author: Miriam Gillinson
description:
Palace theatre, London
Five hours have been trimmed to three for this new version but it is packed with magic moments and superb performances

Ten years on from its premiere, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child has been transformed from an epic two-part play into a richly absorbing one-part production. A similar version is already running to great acclaim on Broadway but it still feels risky to tinker with a show that has come to feel like a fixed jewel in the West End. Happily, that risk has paid off and Cursed Child hasn’t lost any of its sparkle.

Admittedly, there are some drawbacks to reducing Jack Thorne’s ambitious five-hour script into a very tightly packed three hours. The plot can, at times, overwhelm.
title: A one-part wonder! The West End’s streamlined Harry Potter and the Cursed Child works like magic

author: Sasha Muller
description:
Fancy an at-home coffee maker that can grind beans and make tasty espresso? Our expert put 14 to the test, including fully automatic and assisted models

• The best coffee machine for your home

Laziness is akin to godliness. I know this for a fact because, every morning, my kitchen hosts a dishevelled re-enactment of Michelangelo’s famed fresco, the Creazione di Adamo (Creation of Adam). An outstretched arm extends a single finger, and lo – a bean-to-cup machine stirs, a grinder whirs, the smell of freshly ground coffee wafts, coffee drips and milk froths. Hopefully, my cup does not runneth over, for all the big mugs are in the dishwasher.

At its simplest, this is the appeal of a fully automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine. Turn it on, place a cup on the drip tray and lazily prod a
title: The 10 best bean-to-cup coffee machines in the UK, tried and tested

author: Emine Sinmaz
description:
Four women attacked by disgraced comedian say they were left ‘traumatised’, ‘humiliated’ and feeling unsafe, in statements read out in court

  • Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

Victims of Russell Brand have described the lasting impact of his crimes in statements read out at Southwark crown court by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, on Monday. Here are the abbreviated words of the four women, one of whom read out her own statement from behind a screen.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I felt sick at the sight of him parading around’: Russell Brand’s victims on the lifelong impact of his crimes

author: Interviews by Jack Watkins
description:
‘Dressed as knights, we’d walk onstage to the sound of the William Tell overture. I’d quote Henry V and the crowd would shout, “You’re the rightful king of England!”’

I’d worked up the basic idea on Stiff Records’ three-month tour of the northern hemisphere. It’s near-impossible to write songs on the road because you lack the basic solitude, so I’d retire to the tour coach latrine. The melody was really a boogie-blues progression, part-inspired by Norman Greenbaum’s Spirit in the Sky and Canned Heat’s On the Road Again. But lyrics only flowed when we came off the tour. Rehearsing near our favourite drinking haunt, the Castle on Holloway Road, London, provided the opening line: “Deep in the castle and back from the war.”
title: ‘A three-minute history of England written in the tour bus toilet’: how Tenpole Tudor made Swords of a Thousand Men

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
Tate Britain, London
Trying to present these two as pioneers of British art is fruitless: their lives, sexualities and the Picasso and Cézanne paintings in their home were more exciting than what’s here

The Bloomsbury Group once induced yawns as the smug epitome of a snobbish high culture but they’re now admired for their feminism and queer abandon. There’s a West End play about the loves of the Bloomsbury economist John Maynard Keynes and if you visit the National Trust’s Sissinghurst, its flowerbeds are set alight by Vita Sackville-West’s affair with Virginia Woolf.

But biography can’t set art alight, as Tate Britain’s epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings
title: A flaccid roam through Bloomsbury’s desperately mediocre modernists: Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant review

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
David Wilkinson made this warm, generous documentary of his own treatment, and asks why so many much younger people are getting the same diagnosis

‘I am lucky, as I have become old.” That is the pithy, personal summary offered by English film-maker David Wilkinson, whose previous movie was his thoughtful, eloquent film The Marbles, which reopened the case for the restitution of the Parthenon marbles to Greece. Now he reveals that he was in fact battling stage four bowel cancer throughout its making, and this new and very personal film is now about his own condition, a film in which the director is front and centre, speaking candidly to camera in the very midst of his treatment.

In fact, 1 in 2 is specifically about his shock and sadness that so many people alongside him in waiting rooms, or online in bowel cancer discus
title: 1 in 2 review – compassionate film about dealing with bowel cancer is a personal plea on behalf of the young

author: Simon Burnton
description:
• 28-year-old rewarded for county performances

  • Bashir to tour with Lions along with seamer Carse

The uncapped Nottinghamshire spinner Liam Patterson-White has been rewarded for his most productive County Championship season with a call-up to England’s squad for their first red-ball assignment of the winter, the three Tests against South Africa that start in Johannesburg next month.

The potential importance of spin bowling in South Africa was demonstrated in their recent home series against Australia, which the hosts won to propel themselves to No1 in the ICC rankings and in which their most successful bowler was Simon Harmer, who took 14 wickets at 29.35. England will face contrasting conditions, particularly in their first two Tests, and have selected further spin-bowling options in Dan Lawrence, Joe Root and Jacob Bethell, who returns after missing England’s most recent Test series, against Pakistan, through injury, But Shoaib Bashir, a
title: Uncapped Notts spinner Patterson-White earns England Test call-up for South Africa

author: Lucy Pavia
description:
Whether it’s vintage baubles or homemade gifts, there’s joy in a Christmas full of memories and personal touches. Plus, the best coats to keep out the chill this winter

• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

What’s the Christmas decoration you’ve had the longest? Mine is a set of silver paper streamers that originally belonged to my grandparents (and which, if the price in shillings on the original box is anything to go by, pre-date 1971). When I get them out, I can picture my late dad balanced on a chair, pinning them to my childhood dining room ceiling.

It’s the old, slightly broken stuff that makes Christmas: the things you bring out every year, imbued with Christmases past. “I love finding a prime spot on the tree for a little beaded fairy I got at a fair in primary school,” says Filt
title: The best Christmas things aren’t new – and that’s precisely the point

author: Guardian community team
description:
Whether you’re a modeller, actuary or underwriter, we’d like to hear how the insurance industry is dealing with climate risk

With more frequent storms, floods, wildfires and drought, caused by climate change, having a huge impact on property around the world, we’d like to find out how the insurance industry is managing climate change risk.

There have been reports of insurance workers, who analyse risk around a natural disaster, coming under pressure to downplay losses in order to keep premiums affordable for customers. The practice of underestimating risks to keep insurance premiums down could be widespread.

Continue reading...
title: Insurance industry workers: how is climate-related risk managed in your company?

title: Fog envelops large parts of England and Wales – in pictures

author: Emma Beddington
description:
Like many graduates, he has been forced to return to the nest. How will he cope with my pigeon chat and dodgy dregs for dinner?

My graduate son has been back home for five months now. In this economy, he might be stuck here a while longer, meaning we’ve shifted from the extended holiday phase to a new normal. I feel like the William Munny of mothering – a creaky gunslinger dragged out of retirement for one last job, like Clint Eastwood’s character in Unforgiven. Having Seen Things and survived, I had settled into a dourly ascetic afterlife of silent staring and infrequent laundry, measuring out my life in coffee spoons of cholesterol-friendly flaxseed. How rusty am I at mothering? Will I go down in a hail of bullets?

Well, I can still wash, dry and fold multiple loads a week and ensure an uninterrupted supply of milk. It’s muscle memory, instinctive as breathing. I’ve lost other skills, though, like de
title: My son’s back home – and my mothering skills have gone out of the window | Emma Beddington

author: Greg Wood
description:
The 2005 Gambling Act has been described as ‘analogue’ in a digital age and review will be crucial for funding model

The prospect of a new Gambling Act, with significant implications for racing’s funding model via betting, moved a step closer on Monday. A new commission that includes experts from the fields of economics, law, public policy, health and sport will initiate an “independent, evidence-based assessment of the existing [legal] framework [around gambling] and consider whether further reform, including potential new primary legislation, may be required.”

The Gambling Policy Commission (GPC), which is chaired by Jagjit Chadha OBE, a professor of economics at Cambridge University, will launch on Monday with a “call for evidence from all interested parties and individuals”, to be submitted by 12 February 2027. It will then aim to deliver its findings and recommendations before the next general election.
title: Racing must seize its chance as new commission tackles UK betting laws

author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
description:
Ministers pushed to reverse ‘policy madness’ of scrapping exemption on 5% tax rise for heat pumps, solar panels and batteries

Households planning to invest in green energy upgrades, including heat pumps and solar panels, risk a nationwide rush to find an installer or face hundreds of pounds in unexpected costs unless the government abandons its looming VAT increase.

Ministers are under growing pressure to reverse plans to scrap the 5% VAT exemption on home heat pumps, solar panels and batteries from 1 April which could add up to £1,530 on to the cost of a smart home energy system amid record demand for fossil fuel alternatives.

Continue reading...
title: UK households face rush to find green energy installer to beat April VAT hike

author: Cordelia Roche
description:
As the work of Bloomsbury artist Duncan Grant features in a major exhibition, Cordelia Roche reflects on her father’s decades-long relationship with the painter – as friend, muse, but never lover

After Duncan Grant died in our house, in Aldermaston in Berkshire, at the age of 93, I remember my father’s knees buckling and him falling to the ground. It was 1978, the end of their 32-year relationship, and the end of an era.

My father Paul Roche, a poet, writer and translator of Greek plays, seemed to crumble before my eyes. He was 61, a father of five, and I was the youngest. Duncan, the painter, designer and a key figure of the Bloomsbury group, had been his beloved friend for more than half his life.

Continue reading...
title: ‘My father loved Duncan more than he loved us’: the 30-year passion at the heart of the Bloomsbury set – and the family raised in its image

author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
description:
Neso issues ‘electricity margin notice’ for gas power plants on Britain to fire up and boost generation this morning amid energy shortfall

The government body tasked with keeping the lights on has issued a rare call for more electricity supplies this morning due to low wind power generation forecasts across Europe on Monday.

A notice issued by the National Energy System Operator (Neso) on Sunday night said it faced a “shortfall” of almost 1,400 megawatts in its electricity supply margins from 6am until 11am on Monday.

Continue reading...
title: Rare call for more electricity supplies as wind power drops across Europe

author: Anna Tims
description:
I am waiting for the overdue results of a cancer test, and the postal service seems to be prioritising parcels over letters

In the three months since I moved to my village, I’ve had just two deliveries of letters.

One of them was only because I caught a passing postman on a parcel round who arranged one just for me. The bundle contained a bank card, two notifications of an overdue bill I was unaware of, a weeks-old letter from my new water company asking me to set up payments, and a letter about a routine cancer test. There has been nothing since.

Continue reading...
title: Why has Royal Mail only delivered letters twice in three months?

author: Bryan Armen Graham
description:
• British-Somali boxer claims first world titles in Texas

  • Kreps outlands Ali but loses disputed split decision

  • Baumgardner wins 135lb belt as Dubois feud heats up

  • Australia’s Nicolson retains junior featherweight title

British-Somali boxer Ramla Ali became a world champion for the first time at the age of 36 on Sunday night after escaping with a highly contentious 10-round split decision over former sparring partner Mikiah Kreps to claim the vacant WBO and IBF women’s junior featherweight titles in Arlington, Texas.

Ali, who grew up in east London after fleeing Somalia’s civil war with her family and went on to become the first boxer to represent the African country at the Olympics, completed her remarkable journey to the top of the 122lb division at College Park Center on her second attempt at
title: Ramla Ali wins first world titles at 36 with highly controversial split decision

author: Phil Harrison, Hollie Richardson, Jack Seale and Priya Elan
description:
The campaign for justice behind the epilepsy drug that caused damage to generations of children. Plus: shocking sex-outside-marriage revelation in The Gilded Age. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC Two
A still unresolved story of institutional failure and relentless campaigning, this documentary explores the damage done to generations of children by sodium valproate, a drug that was licensed for prescription to people with epilepsy despite concerns having arisen after testing. At the heart of the story are Janet Williams and Emma Murphy, two mothers who refused to be deterred by official inertia (and, at times, outright scorn) and whose robust lack of self-pity makes this film stirring rather than dispiriting. Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: a stirring documentary about two mothers taking on Big Pharma

author: Jack Snape
description:
• One-day international captain Mitch Marsh will face media this week

  • Red ball captain Pat Cummins also expected to face questioning

There is still more to tell about Australian cricket’s ball-tampering controversy according to Usman Khawaja, beyond what is included in his book, as his former teammates steel themselves for their reckoning with a dismayed and disappointed cricket community.

Khawaja wrote in his book Sabr, out on Tuesday, that he urged his teammates to accept collective responsibility for the incident in a 21-page chapter that has resuscitated calls for players – including Test captain Pat Cummins – to address if they had any knowledge about the use of sandpaper to help the ball swing on the 2018 tour of South Africa.

Continue reading...
title: Australian players prepare for fresh grilling after explosive ball tampering claims in Khawaja book

author: Richard Lawson
description:
James Earl Jones theatre, New York City
A ‘mostly true’ tale of 19th-century sisters running from the law is underserved in a production stuffed with superfluous showboating

The new retooled musical Wanted, from writer Angelica Chéri and composer Ross Baum, opens with a blare of excitement: a Greek chorus of sorts, clad in billowing white garments like spirits from the great beyond, lay their scene in 1890s Texas. There, we meet two Black sisters, Mary and Martha Clarke, who will become wanted criminals. The tone of Baum’s music is portentous, its volume high, suggesting that an epic journey is about to unfold. What ensues from there is, sadly, not quite as suspenseful, moving or grand as advertised.

Chéri based this “mostly true” story on two of her great-great aunts, daughters of an emancipated sharecropper whose absent father was white. Mary and Martha are light-skinned and thus figure they can pass in the white world, at least long enough to earn
title: Wanted review – generic crime musical lacks outlaw grit

author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
description:
Stroke Association says widespread lack of rehabilitation hinders patients’ chances of regaining physical and mental function

Fewer than one in 15 stroke survivors are getting the amount of therapy the NHS should provide to maximise their chances of recovery, a report has revealed.

The figure was a “damning” indictment of the widespread lack of rehabilitation for patients, which was hindering their chances of regaining physical and mental function, the Stroke Association said.

Continue reading...
title: Only 6.4% of stroke survivors receive enough therapy, finds ‘damning’ report
